title: Network Theory Numericals 13: AC Power and Power Factor
cover: AC Power and Power Factor Numericals

scenes.narration: Welcome back. Today we calculate AC power. First the three powers and the power triangle for a load. Then a real industrial problem: correcting a motor's power factor with a capacitor, and seeing how much the supply current drops.
scenes.title: AC POWER & POWER FACTOR
scenes.subtitle: Solved problems, step by step

scenes.title: Problem 1 · The three powers
scenes.narration: Problem one. A load draws ten amperes from two hundred and thirty volts at a power factor of zero point eight lagging. Find the real, reactive and apparent power.

scenes.title: Problem 1 · The three powers
scenes.narration: Step one: apparent power is simply V times I, two thousand three hundred volt amperes. Step two: real power is V I cos phi, two thousand three hundred times zero point eight, one thousand eight hundred and forty watts. Step three: for reactive power we need sine phi. Since cos phi is zero point eight, sine phi is the square root of one minus zero point six four, zero point six.

scenes.title: Problem 1 · The three powers
steps: Q = V I sin φ = 2300 × 0.6 = 1380 VAR
scenes.narration: So Q is two thousand three hundred times zero point six, one thousand three hundred and eighty VAR. Check the power triangle: the square root of eighteen forty squared plus thirteen eighty squared is exactly two thousand three hundred. A lagging power factor means the load is inductive, so it absorbs reactive power.

scenes.title: Problem 2 · Power factor correction
scenes.ask:
capacitor kVAR, C,
supply current before/after
scenes.narration: Problem two. A five kilowatt motor runs at a power factor of zero point seven lagging from two hundred and thirty volts, fifty hertz. Find the capacitor needed in parallel to raise the power factor to zero point nine five, and compare the supply current before and after.

scenes.title: Problem 2 · Power factor correction
scenes.narration: Step one: the reactive power now. The angle is the inverse cos of zero point seven, forty five point five seven degrees, and its tangent is one point zero two. Q1 equals P tan phi, five thousand times one point zero two, about five thousand one hundred and one VAR. Step two: the reactive power we want at zero point nine five: the angle is eighteen point one nine degrees, tangent zero point three two nine, so Q2 is about one thousand six hundred and forty three VAR. Step three: the capacitor must supply the difference, about three thousand four hundred and fifty eight VAR.

scenes.title: Problem 2 · Power factor correction
scenes.narration: Step four: the capacitance is Q C over V squared omega: three thousand four hundred and fifty eight divided by two hundred and thirty squared times three fourteen point one six, about two hundred and eight microfarads. Step five: the supply current. Before, five thousand over two thirty times zero point seven, thirty one point one amperes. After, five thousand over two thirty times zero point nine five, twenty two point nine amperes. The motor gets the same five kilowatts, but the cables carry about twenty six percent less current.

Exam tips. Remember S equals V I, P equals V I cos phi, and Q equals V I sine phi. Find sine phi from cos phi with the square root. For power factor correction, use Q equals P tan phi before and after, the capacitor supplies the difference, and C equals Q C over V squared omega. And the capacitor always goes in parallel.
